extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students (practitioners of patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to draft and construe patent specifications and claims so they clearly identify what is new, exclude what is old, and are coextensive with the actual invention; includes rules on drawings, ambiguity, generic claims, and judicial construction. Applicable to preparing specifications and to litigating their sufficiency/scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must state specific improvement and be limited to it
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patent is for an improvement of a machine (or an improved machine) the specification must state in what the improvement specifically consists and the claim must be limited to such improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the terms are so obscure or doubtful that the court cannot say which particular improvement is claimed and to what it is limited, the patent is void for ambiguity; if it covers more than the improvement it is void for being broader than the invention. (See Barrett v. Hall.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings and description must together enable a skilled mechanic
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings are to be read in connection with the words of the specification; together they must explain the invention sufficiently to enable a skilful mechanic to perform the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If, by comparison of words and drawings, the one explains the other sufficiently to enable performance, the specification is sufficient. (See Bloxam v. Elsee.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim prior art as new; distinguish new from old
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification that includes what has been invented before without showing that the patentee does not claim it will render the patent broader than his invention and therefore void; courts cannot reject part of a claim, so any claimed matter that is not new invalidates the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee must state what he claims as new and what he admits to be old; if the description mixes old and new and does not distinctly ascertain what is claimed, the patent will be void. (Carpenter v. Smith; Lowell v. Lewis; Moody v. Fiske.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Constrain claim to be coextensive with actual discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification should be construed, consistently with the fair import of the language, so as to make the claim coextensive with the actual discovery; patentees are presumed not to intend to claim things already in use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literal words may be limited by context (ejusdem generis, state of knowledge, surrounding phrases) so as not to include unrelated matters; courts should avoid forced constructions that extend claims beyond the facts. (Court of Common Pleas rule; Crossley v. Beverly; Winans v. Providence R.R.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmatively state what is new and negatively what is old
rubrics_metrics.description: The usual form is to state affirmatively the patentee's new features, and, when using anything old, to state negatively that he does not claim that thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee is not confined to precise wording, but should sum up and distinguish the invention. Good drafting practice is to describe the whole subject and then point out the parts which are old and those which constitute the improvement. (Wyeth v. Stone; Godson on Patents.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe existing (old) apparatus sufficiently and disclaim it, then state the improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming an improvement, the prior apparatus or machine should be set forth sufficiently to make known what the patentee engrafts his improvement upon; he should disclaim the invention of the old parts and state his improvement distinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to identify the old parts and then state clearly what is added can render the specification defective (illustrated by Nichols v. Ross and Holmes v. L. & N.W.R.W.). The specification should show how the patentee's additions differ from the old structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vagueness in the manner of describing the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A common defect is vagueness or ambiguity in the description that makes it difficult or impossible to determine what the invention is (distinct from mere ambiguous terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: directions that leave uncertain which materials are to be treated (Turner v. Winter); claiming an entire machine by inserting unnecessary parts or numbers (King v. Arkwright). If a whole class is claimed but only one member works, the specification misleads. The specification must enable the public to know what is claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic claims and variations: disclose best modes but claiming equivalents is permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: If a particular effect can be produced in several modes, it is sufficient for the patentee to state the modes he contemplates as best; claiming variations (substitutes of a like character) will not render the claim void so long as the combinations claimed are substantially new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee may claim substitutes or alternative modes of carrying out the invention provided he has invented them or they are substantially new; broad/generic claims are acceptable when they are coextensive with the invention. (Phillips on Patents; Ryan v. Goodwin — matches example.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise with words like 'or' — courts construe by context and state of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Words that appear disjunctive or inclusive (e.g., 'or') must be construed in light of ordinary meaning, the state of knowledge at the patent date, and context; such words can admit either a narrow or broader construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial instructions to fact-finders should avoid absolute pronouncements about equivalence; whether terms are to be read disjunctively or inclusively depends on evidence of how terms were understood at the time. (Elliott v. Turner.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity as to scope (e.g., size, range) invalidates claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification leaves it uncertain whether the claim is for any size (or other broad scope) or only particular sizes/types, that uncertainty can render the specification bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a cable-holder claim uncertain whether for one cable of whatever size or for holders adaptable to different sizes was held defective. (Hastings v. Brown.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts give liberal construction to patents to protect real inventors when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: If, taking the specification as a whole, the court can perceive the exact nature and extent of the claim, it should adopt an interpretation that gives full effect to the inventor's rights rather than defeat them for minor ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle expressed as ut res magis valeat quam pereat: ambiguities should, where reasonable, be resolved to preserve valid claims provided the invention's nature and extent are discernible from the specification as a whole. (Ryan v. Goodwin and related authorities.)
